"The article opens by examining the enduring influence of the 19th-century "great man" theory of history, which proposes that exceptionally talented, charismatic, and courageous individuals shape and direct historical events through the force of their personality and genius alone. Despite the emergence of competing intellectual frameworks—including egalitarian philosophies, Marxist social theory, and EP Thompson's "history from below" approach that gained prominence in the 1960s and emphasized the role of ordinary people—this top-down view of historical change has stubbornly persisted in popular imagination.

The article highlights Scottish philosopher Thomas Carlyle as a key proponent of this theory. Carlyle identified figures such as Aristotle, Julius Caesar, Napoleon, Martin Luther, and the Prophet Muhammad as exemplary heroes who fundamentally and permanently transformed the world around them. According to Carlyle, the broader population could only passively observe, admire, and follow these towering figures who shaped what he termed "universal history."

The author dismisses this concept as foolish yet acknowledges its seductive power and remarkable longevity. The piece then pivots to a critical contemporary observation: there still exist men—and the author emphasizes they are predominantly men—who genuinely believe themselves to be cast in this heroic mold, convinced they possess a special mission, calling, or sacred duty to save peoples and nations. These individuals believe they alone know best, possess unique insight, and are sufficiently ruthless and arrogant to impose their views on everyone else. However, the author argues that in the modern era, such self-styled "great" men are typically not heroes at all but rather anti-heroes or, more accurately, villains who nonetheless wield significant power similar to Carlyle's chosen few."
